STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, relatable problem with a tangible reuse angle; glass jars have real residual value and the sustainability trend supports interest. (2) Sensible niche focus on small and independent candle makers, who lack resources to build their own reuse loops and are underserved by large-brand programs and generic packaging-reuse services. (3) Three-part solution (mailer, cleaning/refill, dashboard) is coherent, and the dashboard adds a marketing/storytelling benefit for makers. (4) Candid, self-aware plan: the team openly names gaps (no market sizing, pricing, financial model, entity) and correctly identifies the real competitor as customer inertia. (5) Complementary student team (operations/environment, industrial design, information systems) with early prototype work and a few real users, showing initiative at very low cost. (6) Modest, sensible use of funds (entity, website, pilot) and openness to mentorship.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Unit economics are the central risk and are unvalidated. Round-trip postage on heavy glass, mailer cost, cleaning labor, and inspection/breakage likely exceed the price of a new wholesale jar (often well under $1-3), so the claim that a per-jar fee will beat new-jar cost is doubtful and untested. Shipping glass twice also undermines the carbon-savings story, which is not supported by any lifecycle analysis. (2) Return-rate risk: the plan itself concedes people will not bother, yet there is no incentive design (deposits, discounts, credits) and no data on actual return rates; low returns would starve the model of volume. (3) Operational complexity: wax removal, sanitizing, chip/crack inspection, and reverse logistics are labor-intensive and hard to scale from a shared kitchen; jars vary by maker, causing sorting and compatibility issues; regulatory/safety and wax-disposal considerations are unaddressed. (4) Weak market evidence: no sizing, no count of target makers, no willingness-to-pay data; 'positive feedback' from friends/family is low-signal and no paying customers or revenue exist. (5) Two-sided/three-party coordination (makers, consumers, Wickedgood) requires maker adoption and workflow changes, and small makers have thin margins and low volume per maker, making customer acquisition costly relative to revenue per account. (6) Competitive defensibility is thin: a candle-only focus is easy for others to replicate, and a dashboard is not a durable moat. (7) Execution constraints: part-time student founders, no legal entity, no website, no advisors, and no financial model or defined pricing. Overall: a worthy, sympathetic idea at a very early stage whose viability hinges on unproven economics and consumer behavior; interest is moderate-to-low pending pilot data on return rates, cost per jar, and maker willingness to pay.
